questions.stem: The earliest cities of Mesopotamia, Egypt, the Indus Valley and China all grew up beside major rivers. The main reason was that the rivers provided:
options: a steady climate with rain falling evenly all year round
water and fertile silt for farming, and a route for trade
natural defences that made walls and armies unnecessary
the only source of the stone needed for building temples
questions.explanation: Flooding rivers laid down fertile silt and supplied water for irrigation, which allowed surpluses that could feed large populations, and the rivers also carried goods. These societies still built walls and armies, and southern Mesopotamia in fact lacked building stone.

questions.stem: The Indus Valley civilisation grew up on the floodplains of the Indus and a second river system to the east, now largely dry. Which modern countries contain most of its sites?
options: Pakistan and north-western India
Iran and Afghanistan
Bangladesh and the eastern states of India
Iraq and Syria
questions.explanation: Most Indus sites lie in Pakistan, including Harappa and Mohenjo-daro, and in north-western India, including Lothal, Dholavira and Rakhigarhi. Iraq and Syria were the heartland of Mesopotamia.

questions.stem: Excavations at Mehrgarh, at the foot of the Bolan Pass in Balochistan, are significant for the study of the Indus Valley because they show:
options: that the Indus cities were founded by settlers sent from Sumer
the earliest examples of the Indus script carved on large stone stelae
a royal cemetery of Indus kings buried with their attendants
farming villages there long before the Indus cities arose
questions.explanation: From about 7000 BCE Mehrgarh had farmers growing wheat and barley and herding animals, showing a long local development before the cities. This counts against the old idea that Indus civilisation was simply brought from Mesopotamia.

questions.stem: Mesopotamia, Egypt, the Indus Valley, China and Mesoamerica all developed farming and later cities, mostly without any contact at the start. What does this pattern best suggest about the origins of settled societies?
options: Only river valleys with a cold climate could support early farming
Similar conditions led different peoples to settle independently
Settled life began in one region and was copied by all the others
Cities came first, and farming was invented later to feed them
questions.explanation: Farming and urban life arose separately in several regions, which points to similar pressures and opportunities rather than one source spreading outwards. Farming villages came long before cities everywhere, and these regions were warm, not cold.

questions.stem: The Indus Valley civilisation is often called the Harappan civilisation because:
options: Harappa was the first of its cities to be excavated
Harappa was its capital, named in the Indus script on many seals
a king named Harappa is recorded as its founder in Sumerian texts
Harappa is the only one of its sites where writing has been found
questions.explanation: Archaeologists name a culture after its first-studied type site, and Harappa was excavated before Mohenjo-daro. The script is undeciphered, so no capital or king can be read from it, and inscribed seals come from many sites.

questions.stem: In the 1850s, railway builders took large numbers of bricks from the mound at Harappa to use as track ballast. Why is this important for archaeologists today?
options: Much of the upper city was destroyed before it could be recorded
The bricks were later returned and rebuilt in their original places
It led directly to the first scientific excavation of the site
The damage revealed the royal tombs buried beneath the city
questions.explanation: Brick robbing for the Lahore to Multan railway removed much of Harappa's later structures, so evidence was lost before excavation began. Proper excavation came only in the 1920s, and no royal tombs have been found at Harappa.

questions.stem: Alexander Cunningham, of the Archaeological Survey of India, visited Harappa in the nineteenth century. Which find did he publish?
options: A bilingual tablet in Indus script and cuneiform
The bronze figure known as the Dancing Girl
A stone statue later named the Priest-King
A seal with an unknown script and a carved bull
questions.explanation: Cunningham published a seal from Harappa bearing a bull and signs he could not read, but he did not realise how old it was. The Dancing Girl and the Priest-King were found later at Mohenjo-daro, and no bilingual text has ever been found.

questions.stem: Which statement about the excavations of the 1920s is correct?
options: John Marshall dug at Ur and Mortimer Wheeler at Mohenjo-daro
Heinrich Schliemann dug at Harappa and Arthur Evans at Lothal
Daya Ram Sahni dug at Harappa and R. D. Banerji at Mohenjo-daro
Leonard Woolley dug at Harappa and Howard Carter at Mohenjo-daro
questions.explanation: Sahni excavated at Harappa in 1921 and Banerji began at Mohenjo-daro in 1922. John Marshall, Director-General of the Archaeological Survey of India, realised the two sites belonged to one culture and announced the discovery in 1924. Woolley worked at Ur.

questions.stem: John Marshall announced the discovery of the Indus civilisation in 1924. Which evidence most clearly showed that Harappa and Mohenjo-daro, some 600 km apart, belonged to one culture?
options: A road between the cities found by aerial survey
Identical temples to the same god at both sites
Matching seals, script, bricks and pottery
Inscriptions naming the same king at both cities
questions.explanation: The same seal types, signs, standard bricks and pottery appeared at both sites, showing a shared culture across a huge area. No king's name can be read in the script and no clearly identified temples have been found.

questions.stem: In the 1940s Mortimer Wheeler interpreted the raised mound at Harappa as a fortified 'citadel' and a large building there as a 'granary'. Why do many archaeologists now question these labels?
options: The building was discovered to be a modern structure made of railway bricks
They borrowed ideas from Roman and Near Eastern sites without proof
Later digs found the building full of grain, so it must have been a temple
Radiocarbon dating proved the mound was built after the city was abandoned
questions.explanation: Wheeler, trained on Roman Britain, expected citadels and state granaries, but no grain has been found in the Harappa 'granary' and the platform may have been a hall or storehouse of some other kind. The labels reflect his assumptions as much as the evidence.

questions.stem: Since the 1980s, projects such as the Harappa Archaeological Research Project have changed how Indus sites are studied. Which approach is typical of this newer work?
options: Clearing whole mounds quickly in search of royal tombs and treasure
Relying mainly on later Sanskrit texts to explain what was found
Removing standing buildings to reach the lowest layers faster
Small, careful trenches and the study of crafts and daily life
questions.explanation: Recent teams use controlled excavation, dating, and the study of animal bones, plant remains and workshops to reconstruct how ordinary people lived. Large clearances of the kind made in the 1920s destroyed context, and Sanskrit texts date from much later.

questions.stem: Which feature is typical of Mohenjo-daro and Harappa?
options: Grid-planned streets with covered brick drains
A great ziggurat rising at the centre of each city
Houses built of cut stone around a royal palace
Massive pyramid tombs on the edge of the desert
questions.explanation: Indus cities had main streets running roughly north-south and east-west, with drains along them and household drains feeding in. Ziggurats belong to Mesopotamia and pyramids to Egypt, and Indus houses were built of brick, not cut stone.

questions.stem: Indus baked bricks were made to standard proportions of about 1:2:4 (thickness to width to length) at sites hundreds of kilometres apart. What does this best suggest?
options: Shared rules or authority guided building across the region
All bricks were made in one city and carried to the others
Building methods were copied from Egyptian pyramid builders
Each family designed its own bricks to suit its own house
questions.explanation: The same proportions at many sites point to shared standards, whether set by rulers, guilds or tradition. Bricks were made locally, as kilns and clay sources show, and Indus building owed nothing to Egyptian stone pyramids.

questions.stem: The Great Bath at Mohenjo-daro was:
options: a burial pool where the bodies of rulers were placed after death
a large brick tank made watertight with bitumen
a public swimming pool for athletes training for military games
a stone reservoir that supplied drinking water to the lower town
questions.explanation: The Great Bath, about 12 m long and 7 m wide, had steps at each end and was sealed with gypsum mortar and a layer of bitumen. Many scholars think it was used for ritual bathing, though its exact purpose is unknown.

questions.stem: Most houses at Mohenjo-daro had a bathing area and a drain, but archaeologists have identified no grand palace, royal tomb or obvious temple. Which conclusion is most defensible?
options: The cities had no organised authority, since nobody planned the streets or drains
Power may have been held by elites who did not display it as kings did
The Indus cities had no social differences, since all houses were the same size
The rulers' palaces must lie under the Great Bath and will be found by digging
questions.explanation: Large-scale planning, drainage and standard weights show organised authority, yet rulers left no obvious monuments, so many archaeologists suggest councils, merchants or ritual leaders rather than kings. House sizes do vary, so the society was not equal in every way.

questions.stem: At Dholavira in Gujarat, archaeologists found large stone-cut reservoirs and channels. This evidence best shows that Indus communities:
options: depended on monsoon floods from the Ganges
built dams to drown rival cities upstream
used canals mainly to defend the city walls
managed scarce water carefully in a dry region
questions.explanation: Dholavira lies in the dry Rann of Kutch, and its reservoirs stored monsoon run-off for a growing town. It shows how Indus planning adapted to local conditions, not that water was used as a weapon.

questions.stem: Indus seals were usually small squares of carved steatite showing an animal, often a 'unicorn', and a short line of signs. They were mainly used to:
options: print long religious texts on sheets of cloth and palm leaf
record the names of the dead carved on their burial stones
stamp clay sealings on goods to mark ownership
mint coins with a fixed value for use in the city markets
questions.explanation: Impressions of seals survive on clay tags that once sealed bags and bundles, showing their role in trade and administration. The Indus civilisation had no coinage, and its inscriptions are far too short for long texts.

questions.stem: Why has the Indus script not been deciphered?
options: Its inscriptions are very short and no bilingual text has been found
Archaeologists have found fewer than twenty inscribed objects in total
It was written in an alphabet identical to the one used for Sanskrit
The tablets were destroyed by Wheeler before scholars could study them
questions.explanation: Several thousand inscribed objects survive, but most carry only about five signs and there is nothing like the Rosetta Stone pairing it with a known script. Its language is unknown, and it is not related to later scripts used for Sanskrit.

questions.stem: Mesopotamian cuneiform was deciphered, while the Indus script remains unread. How does this affect the study of the two civilisations?
options: Indus politics and beliefs must be inferred mostly from material remains
Indus history is better known because archaeology is more reliable than texts
Mesopotamian history is unknown because its tablets were too short to read
Both are known equally well because their seals carry the same symbols
questions.explanation: Historians of Sumer can read rulers' names, laws and accounts, but for the Indus they must rely on buildings, objects and their contexts, so ideas about government and religion stay tentative. The two regions used quite different seals and writing.

questions.stem: Cubes of polished chert found at many Indus sites follow a set system of weights, doubling at first (1, 2, 4, 8 and so on) and then rising in larger steps. What does this best show?
options: The weights were children's toys used for counting games
Indus merchants borrowed their weights from Roman traders
Trade and taxation used agreed standards across a wide area
Every city used its own different system of measuring goods
questions.explanation: The same graded weights appear from the Indus to Gujarat, pointing to standardised exchange, perhaps overseen by an authority. Rome did not exist for another two thousand years, and the careful grading rules out toys.

questions.stem: The small bronze figure from Mohenjo-daro known as the 'Dancing Girl' is evidence that Indus craft workers:
options: used iron tools to shape their statues
could cast metal using the lost-wax method
carved large stone statues of their kings
learned bronze working from Shang China
questions.explanation: The figure was cast by modelling in wax, covering it in clay and replacing the melted wax with molten metal. Indus craftsmen worked in copper and bronze, not iron, and Shang bronze working came later.

questions.stem: Craft workshops at Indus sites made beads of carnelian, shell ornaments and stoneware bangles to very high standards. Historians use this evidence mainly to argue that Indus cities had:
options: no farmers, since everyone worked in the workshops
a coinage system to pay workers for each bead made
slaves captured from Egypt to do all skilled work
full-time specialists fed by a farming surplus
questions.explanation: Long drilled carnelian beads took great skill and time, which points to specialists fed by surplus grain, a defining feature of civilisation. Most people still farmed, and there was no coinage.

questions.stem: Remains of cloth from Mohenjo-daro are among the earliest evidence anywhere for the use of which fibre?
options: Linen
Hemp
Cotton
Silk
questions.explanation: Traces of cotton textile found at Mohenjo-daro are among the earliest evidence of cotton use. Silk was produced in China, and linen, made from flax, was widely used in Egypt and Mesopotamia.

questions.stem: The Early Dynastic period in Sumer, about 2900 to 2350 BCE, is best described as a time of:
options: Assyrian rule from the capital at Nineveh
Egyptian control of the cities of the south
rival city-states such as Ur, Lagash and Umma
a single empire ruled from Babylon by Hammurabi
questions.explanation: In the Early Dynastic period independent city-states, each with its patron god, competed for land and water. Sargon of Akkad united them only at the end of the period, and Hammurabi and the Assyrian kings came much later.

questions.stem: The Stele of the Vultures records a victory of Eannatum of Lagash over the neighbouring city of Umma. It is useful evidence that Early Dynastic city-states:
options: settled every dispute through Hammurabi's laws
fought one another over borders and farmland
were united under one king in a lasting peace
sent their armies mainly against the Indus cities
questions.explanation: The stele records a long border conflict between Lagash and Umma over fertile land, with the god of Lagash shown as the victor. It shows rivalry between cities and the use of religion to justify war.

questions.stem: The Sumerian King List presents kingship passing from one city to another, with some early kings reigning for thousands of years. How should a historian use it?
options: Carefully, as a later work blending legend and history into one line of rule
As an exact record of reign lengths, since it was copied from royal archives
Not at all, since all of the kings it names have been proved to be fictional
As the best evidence of the Indus kings, since it lists rulers from Meluhha
questions.explanation: The list was compiled long after the Early Dynastic period and treats kingship as if only one city held it at a time, though cities ruled side by side. Some kings it names, such as Mesannepada of Ur, appear in contemporary inscriptions, so it is not wholly fictional.

questions.stem: Which comparison of Early Dynastic Ur and Mohenjo-daro is best supported by the evidence?
options: Ur was built of stone on hills; Mohenjo-daro was built of reeds on water
Ur had royal burials and temples; Mohenjo-daro has planning but no royal display
Both cities left long written law codes that name their rulers and their gods
Mohenjo-daro had a great ziggurat and royal tombs; Ur had none of either
questions.explanation: Ur's Royal Cemetery and temple precinct display the power of kings and gods, while Mohenjo-daro's drains, grid and Great Bath show organisation without obvious monuments to rulers. Both were built mainly of mud brick, and neither left a law code from this period.

questions.stem: An inscription of Sargon of Akkad boasts that ships from Dilmun, Magan and Meluhha moored at his capital. Most scholars identify Meluhha as:
options: the Indus Valley region
the island of Crete
the Nile Delta in Egypt
the Yellow River valley
questions.explanation: Mesopotamian texts describe Meluhha as a distant land supplying carnelian, ivory, fine woods and other goods, which fits the Indus region. Dilmun is usually identified with Bahrain and Magan with Oman, stages along the Gulf route.

questions.stem: Which archaeological find best supports trade between Mesopotamia and the Indus Valley?
options: Indus-style seals and etched carnelian beads found at Ur
Egyptian scarabs found in the Great Bath at Mohenjo-daro
Cuneiform tablets naming the kings buried at Harappa
Chinese bronze vessels found in the Royal Cemetery of Ur
questions.explanation: Seals in Indus style and etched carnelian beads of Indus type have been found at Ur and other Mesopotamian cities, matching texts about Meluhha. No cuneiform text names Indus kings, and there was no contact with Shang China at this time.

questions.stem: At Lothal in Gujarat, the excavator S. R. Rao interpreted a large brick-lined basin as a dockyard. Why is this interpretation debated?
options: Some argue the basin was a water reservoir rather than a dock for ships
The basin was later shown to be a Roman harbour built many centuries later
No Indus seals or beads of any kind have been found anywhere at Lothal
Lothal lies high in the Himalayas, far from any river or sea route
questions.explanation: Lothal lay near the coast and had bead workshops and seals, so trade is clear, but critics question whether ships could enter the basin and suggest it stored water. The debate shows how one feature can support more than one reading.

questions.stem: Many Indus cities were in decline or abandoned by about:
options: 3300 BCE
500 CE
1900 BCE
questions.explanation: The Mature Harappan phase is usually dated about 2600 to 1900 BCE, after which the big cities shrank and people moved to smaller settlements, especially further east and south. 3300 BCE is the start of the early Harappan phase.

questions.stem: Mortimer Wheeler suggested that invading Aryans destroyed Mohenjo-daro, pointing to skeletons found lying in the streets. Why is this theory now rejected by most archaeologists?
options: Excavations showed the city was destroyed by a single volcanic eruption
Later texts prove that the Aryans arrived about a thousand years before the city
The skeletons came from different periods and few showed violent injuries
DNA tests proved the skeletons belonged to soldiers sent from Sumer by Sargon
questions.explanation: Later study, notably by George Dales in the 1960s, showed the skeletons were not from a single massacre layer and few had battle wounds, and there is no burnt destruction layer. Most scholars now see a gradual decline with several causes.

questions.stem: Which combination of causes is most widely put forward for the decline of the Indus cities?
options: A volcanic eruption that buried Harappa and Mohenjo-daro in ash
A plague brought by Roman merchants arriving at Lothal by sea
Shifting rivers, a weaker monsoon and the loss of long-distance trade
A single enemy invasion followed by the burning of every major city
questions.explanation: Evidence points to changes in river courses, including the drying of the river system east of the Indus, a weakening monsoon, and a fall in trade with Mesopotamia. People did not vanish but moved to smaller villages, so the change was gradual.

questions.stem: Some writers have identified a seal from Mohenjo-daro showing a seated, horned figure surrounded by animals as an early form of the Hindu god Shiva. Why should historians treat this claim with caution?
options: Without readable texts, the figure's identity is guessed from later beliefs
The seal was proved to be a fake made by railway workers in the nineteenth century
Hindu texts clearly state that Shiva was first worshipped in Mesopotamia
The figure is plainly labelled in the Indus script as a king, not a god
questions.explanation: Reading a much later god back into an image more than a thousand years older risks imposing later beliefs on the evidence, and the script cannot confirm who the figure is. This shows how interpretation fills gaps in undeciphered evidence.
